extracted.intended_audience: registered patent & trademark practitioners and attorneys who practice before the USPTO
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and obligations governing practitioner conduct in trademark practice before the USPTO, including requirements for specimens, signatures, representation by U.S. counsel, supervision of non-practitioners, and related professional conduct rules and sanctions. The page is a Final Order describing violations, legal conclusions, and required remedial steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: U.S. Counsel Rule (Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for foreign trademark applicants and registrants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants, registrants, or parties to a trademark proceeding whose domicile is not located within the U.S. or its territories must be represented by an attorney who is an active member in good standing of the bar of the highest court of a state in the U.S. (Requirement of U.S. Licensed Attorney for Foreign Trademark Applicants and Registrants, 84 FR 31498; 37 C.F.R. § 2.11(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Became effective August 3, 2019. Implemented in response to unauthorized practice of law by foreign representatives and to improve accuracy and integrity of the trademark register. Intended to increase customer compliance with U.S. trademark law and regulations; practitioners who represent trademark applicants before the USPTO are expected to undertake a bona fide review of specimens submitted in support of an application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark specimen requirement (use in commerce)
rubrics_metrics.description: A trademark application filed under section 1(a) must include a specimen showing the mark as used on or in connection with the goods or services listed in the application (37 C.F.R. § 2.56). The specimen must show the mark in 'use in commerce,' defined as bona fide use of the mark in the ordinary course of trade, not merely to reserve a right in the mark (15 U.S.C. § 1127; TMEP § 901).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mock-ups or representations of how the mark will appear in sale or advertising are not proper specimens (TMEP §§ 904.03(a), 904.04). Material inserted into a package is not a proper specimen (TMEP § 904.04(c)). The TMEP advises that a reasonable inquiry may be appropriate when the specimen consists of a photograph of the mark reproduced on a plain white label adhered to the goods or printed packaging (TMEP § 904.03(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on mock-ups and improper specimen types
rubrics_metrics.description: A mock-up or representation of how the mark will appear in the sale or advertising of the goods or services is not a proper specimen; material inserted into a package is not proper (TMEP §§ 904.03(a), 904.04; TMEP § 904.04(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must ensure specimens actually depict bona fide use in commerce; frequent submission of mocked-up or digitally altered specimens can undermine the register's integrity and render registrations potentially invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Certification of evidentiary support and reasonable inquiry (37 C.F.R. § 11.18)
rubrics_metrics.description: By filing a trademark application, the practitioner certifies that '[t]o the best of the [practitioner's] knowledge, information and belief, formed after an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances' the allegations and representations in the application have evidentiary support (37 C.F.R. § 11.18).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must conduct a reasonable inquiry before filing; the TMEP specifically notes that such an inquiry may be appropriate when the specimen is a photograph of the mark on a plain white label (TMEP § 904.03(a)). Failure to conduct a reasonable inquiry violates § 11.18 and may be prejudicial to the integrity of the trademark system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademark signature rules and electronic signature requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All signatures must be personally entered by the named signatory; a person electronically signing must personally enter any combination of letters, numbers, spaces, and/or punctuation adopted as a signature, placed between two forward slash ('/') symbols in the signature block on the electronic submission (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.193(a) and (c), and 37 C.F.R. § 11.18(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USPTO guidance (TMEP § 611.01(c)) unequivocally proscribes anyone other than the named signatory from signing electronic trademark documents. 'The person(s) identified as the signatory must manually enter the elements of the electronic signature. Another person (e.g., paralegal, legal assistant, or secretary) may not sign the name of a qualified practitioner or other authorized signatory.' Typing another person's electronic signature is not valid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarations signed under penalty of perjury and criminal liability for false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademark applications contain declarations signed under penalty of perjury; false statements are subject to punishment under 18 U.S.C. § 1001. Signatories make specific representations regarding the applicants' use of the mark in commerce and/or intent to use the mark in commerce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the USPTO relies on these declarations when examining applications and issuing registrations, practitioners must ensure the representations are truthful and supported by inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practitioner competence (37 C.F.R. § 11.101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall provide competent representation (37 C.F.R. § 11.101).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competence includes knowing and understanding applicable rules such as the U.S. Counsel Rule, specimen rules, and signature rules; failure to know these rules leading to violations constitutes lack of competence under § 11.101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable diligence and promptness (37 C.F.R. § 11.103)
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner shall act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client (37 C.F.R. § 11.103).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes taking reasonable steps to ensure clients' filings were prepared, reviewed, signed, and filed in compliance with the U.S. Counsel Rule, specimen rules, and signature rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communications with client (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a) and (b))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners must communicate with clients; specifically, they must inform clients of matters such that clients can make informed decisions (37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a), 11.104(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to inform clients, directly or through associates, of actual or potential adverse consequences of noncompliance with the U.S. Counsel Rule, specimen rules, and signature rules violates these communication obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsibilities regarding non-practitioner assistance (37 C.F.R. § 11.503(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner must supervise and take responsibility for non-practitioner assistance; authorizing or allowing non-practitioners to prepare drafts of trademark documents without adequate supervision violates § 11.503(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners who rely on foreign intermediaries must ensure adequate supervision so documents prepared by non-practitioners include proper specimens and comply with USPTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assisting unauthorized practice before the USPTO in trademark matters (37 C.F.R. § 11.505)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assisting or authorizing non-practitioners to communicate with clients or provide advice about trademark matters (e.g., specimens) that constitutes unauthorized practice violates § 11.505.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitting non-practitioners to advise clients or otherwise participate in practice before the Office can amount to assisting unauthorized practice and is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the U.S. trademark registration system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner conduct that undermines the integrity of the trademark registration system—such as failing to comply with the U.S. Counsel Rule, signature rules, or § 11.18 reasonable inquiry requirement—is conduct prejudicial to the integrity of the U.S. trademark registration system (37 C.F.R. § 11.804(d)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such conduct can be the basis for disciplinary action because the USPTO relies on practitioner-submitted documents when examining applications and issuing registrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obligation to know the client identity when working with intermediaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a trademark practitioner works with a foreign intermediary, the client remains the trademark applicant (Responsibilities of Practitioners Representing Clients in Proceedings Before The Patent and Trademark Office).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners are expected to know the identities of their clients and take reasonable steps to avoid foreseeable prejudice to clients' rights; receiving instructions through an agent does not change who the client is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to provide bar information when representing applicants and registrants
rubrics_metrics.description: U.S. attorneys representing applicants and registrants must provide their bar information when representing applicants and registrants, whether domiciled inside or outside the U.S. (37 C.F.R. §§ 2.17(b)(3), 2.32(a)(4)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Providing accurate bar information supports accountability and enforcement of the U.S. Counsel Rule and related professional obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reinstatement conditions and remedial education (conditions for return to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a condition of reinstatement after suspension, a practitioner may be required to: complete specified continuing legal education on ethics/professional responsibility (here, eight hours), review TMEP provisions including signature requirements, comply with 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.58 and 11.60, and serve a probationary period as ordered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The OED Director may require sworn affidavits or verified declarations and evidence demonstrating completion of education and review; failure to comply during probation may prompt additional suspension proceedings.
